name: Indian Yellow
lede: Indian yellow is a deep, glowing golden yellow watercolor pigment that came from India in hard, foul-smelling balls, and its reputed source, the urine of mango-fed cows, is one of the best-known stories in the history of color, and one of the shakiest.

sections.title: The name and the swatch
sections.body:
*Indian yellow* names a pigment first and a color second. Its warm, almost orange-gold shade is the point of the name: Ball calls the ground pigment a deep golden yellow [1]. In Europe the name came from the trade route, because the balls arrived from India, but the Indian names are older and more varied [1][4].

The swatch here is the dictionary color: ISCC-NBS 1955 calls it a moderate orange yellow, block 68, and lists Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary as a source, with 1735 as the first recorded use of the name [14]. It is a screen value for a pigment that no longer exists in its original form [14]. Paterson's dictionary describes the color as a vivid golden yellow [6]. Maerz and Paul also gave an unexplained alternative, *snowshoe yellow*, whose origin is obscure [4].

Close neighbors in our data include [[golden-yellow]], [[marigold]], [[mustard]], [[ochre]] and [[apricot]], and the French and English trade often used the name for a hue as much as for a substance [14][12].

sections.title: What it was made of
sections.body:
The coloring matter of Indian yellow is a calcium or magnesium salt of euxanthic acid, a compound of the xanthone family [4]. Ball adds that the acid is released by the mango, and that urine is only an incidental component [1].

The recipe usually repeated is this: cows fed only on mango leaves produced urine that was collected in small earthen pots and boiled down. The sediment was strained and rolled by hand into balls, which were dried over charcoal and then left in the sun [4][3]. The raw product was crude and needed refining before painters could use it [4].

Once ground, the pigment is better than its raw balls suggest. Ball describes it as rather lovely, with properties better suited to watercolor than to oil [1]. That suits the world it came from, because most of the paintings that used it were small works on paper [3][7].

sections.title: Piuri, peori and gogili
sections.body:
In India the pigment had a crowd of names, most of them spellings of one word [4]. The Pigment Compendium lists piuri, peori, purree, puri, pioury, peoli and Monghyr puri, together with gogili and gaugoli [4]. Ball dates the Indian use of the name *purree* or *peori* to about the fifteenth century [1].

Gogili is the most suggestive of these. Chandra, cited in the Compendium, reads it as an Indianized form of a Persian term meaning "cow earth", and argues from this that the pigment began in Persia [4]. Coles repeats the "cow earth" reading and says it may offer a clue about where the pigment was first invented [5]. Ball also thinks the pigment seems to be of Persian origin [1].

Books disagree on the date and the hands. Ball puts its Indian use at about the fifteenth century, while Finlay writes that it was most likely invented by Persians in the late sixteenth century and used first by Mughal artists, then by Hindu and Jain painters [1][2]. The Compendium gives a wide window, from the fifteenth to the nineteenth century, and calls India the main place of production [4]. Nobody has pinned the origin down.

sections.title: In Indian painting
sections.body:
St Clair notes that many Indian painters, especially in the Rajasthani and Pahari traditions, used the pigment in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, though both its origin and the end of its use remain unclear [3]. Jarman lists it as the bright yellow of Indian miniatures [7].

Finlay opens her account in the Prince of Wales Museum in Mumbai, with an eighteenth-century watercolor of Krishna and Radha under a mango tree [2]. Krishna's yellow dhoti, she says, may well be painted with Indian yellow [2]. The scene includes cows, mango leaves and yellow cloth in one picture, and she reads it as the story of the paint in miniature [2]. This is her speculation, not a technical identification of the pigment.

Finlay also notes the irony that Jain painters, who are vegetarians and strongly opposed to harming animals, are said to have used a color whose making was supposedly cruel [2]. The tension is real only if the cow story is true.

sections.title: Into Europe
sections.body:
Ball says it is not known exactly when Dutch traders began to import the golden material [1]. Some Dutch paintings of the 1600s contain it, but it seems to have spread more widely through Europe only in the late 1700s [1]. St Clair, by contrast, dates its journey to Europe to the late 1700s [3]. The two accounts are compatible if early use was rare, but the first Western date is not settled [1][3].

It arrived as a trade good alongside gamboge, which Ball says the East India Company imported from about 1615 and which came from the resin of *Garcinia* trees in South-East Asia [1]. The two yellows were rivals. St Clair calls Indian yellow a product of trade and empire that closely resembled gamboge [3]. Both fade, and both work best as watercolors [1].

The shipments arrived in parcels at London docks from Calcutta, addressed to colormen such as George Field and Winsor and Newton [2]. St Clair adds that the recipients could guess the contents the moment they began unwrapping, because of the ammonia smell [3].

sections.title: What the smell suggested
sections.body:
The smell started the speculation. Mérimée, a French colorman, noted that the pigment smelled of urine but would not accept that it could contain any [1][3]. Field, the English colorman, argued that it came from the urine of camels, though he allowed that others ascribed it to the buffalo or the Indian cow [3][2]. Ball adds that some even deemed it a product of snakes [1].

A German chemist named W. Schmidt stated in 1855 that it came from camels that had eaten mango fruit [2]. The New Pocket Cyclopaedia of 1813 said only that it was thought to be an animal secretion [3]. The English artist Roger Dewhurst was told in the 1780s that it was possibly made from animals' urine, and was advised to wash the pigment well before use [3].

Field disliked the pigment for a different reason. Finlay says it was not the smell but the fast fading that bothered him [2]. Gurney's modern list of pigments to avoid still puts Indian yellow among the historic or not recommended colors [11].

sections.title: Mukharji's letter, 1883
sections.body:
On 31 January 1883, Sir Joseph Hooker, director of Kew Gardens, wrote to the India Office to ask what Indian yellow was made of [3]. The answer came from Trailokyanath Mukharji, a civil servant of about 36, and reached Kew some nine and a half months later [3]. The Journal of the Society of Arts published his report in 1883 [3][2].

By his account, the pigment was made in only one place, Mirzapur, a small suburb of Monghyr in Bihar [1][2]. A small group of herdsmen, the *gwalas*, kept cows on a diet of mango leaves and water [3]. Each cow gave about three quarts of luminous yellow urine a day, which they boiled down every night [3]. The yellow solid was pressed into lumps, dried and sent on to Calcutta and Patna [1].

Mukharji also reported that the cows looked unhealthy and were said to die early, and that the herdsmen made them pass water on demand by rubbing the animals by hand [2]. Ball reports that regular dairy farmers disliked the practice and called the herdsmen "cow-destroyers" [1]. Mukharji sent Hooker balls of pigment, a pot, mango leaves and a urine sample on 22 November 1883, and the pigment, still faintly smelly, remains in Kew's archive [3].

sections.title: Banned for cruelty? What is and is not known
sections.body:
The story that Indian yellow was banned for cruelty is told with confidence in several books [1][7], and it is a claim to be treated with care. Ball says Bengal had legislation against cruelty to animals by 1890 that made the manufacture illegal, and that the pigment had all but gone by 1908 [1]. Jarman is blunter, noting that it was banned [7].

Finlay looked for the law and could not find it. She searched the India Library in London and the National Library in Calcutta, and found no records of such laws, no newspaper articles and no correspondence [2]. The four researchers who wrote the Indian yellow chapter in the National Gallery of Art's pigment series found none either [2]. St Clair agrees that it was believed to have been outlawed but that no record could be found [3]. The Compendium sums up that documentary sources diverge, while allowing that production appears to have been halted at least in part for this reason [4].

The mango-cow story itself is not beyond doubt. Contemporary British surveys of the region, careful enough to count cows and buffaloes, never mention the pigment or its herd [2][3]. When Finlay visited Mirzapur in 2002, nobody remembered piuri, and the villagers laughed at her mime of the process [2][3]. She also reports that a violin maker who tried the recipe got a color that was not at all intense [2]. St Clair finds Mukharji credible, since he was a civil servant who had compiled catalogs for exhibitions in Amsterdam and Glasgow, and since he sent physical samples [3].

So the careful position is this: a pigment called piuri was made in Bihar and sold in India and abroad, and Mukharji's report describes how [3][4]. Whether it was made exactly as he said, and whether a law ended it, are not established [2][3][4]. Paterson's dictionary states the cow-and-mango recipe as plain fact, and Jarman repeats the ban, which shows how easily the story hardens [6][7].

sections.title: Euxanthic acid and its imitations
sections.body:
Chemists named the colorant after the pigment: euxanthic acid and its parent compound euxanthone are xanthones, a family that also includes the colorants of gamboge and dragon's blood [4]. The Colour Index lists Indian yellow as CI 75320 [4].

By the end of the pigment's life the name no longer guaranteed the substance. The Compendium notes that cobalt yellow, sold as aureolin, was also marketed as Indian yellow, and that tubes labeled with the name may contain azo yellow dyes instead [4]. Ball makes the general point: manufacturers treated names such as Indian yellow, vermilion and cobalt blue as designations of a hue rather than a substance [12].

Doerner advised painters in the 1930s to replace golden Indian yellow with a synthetic Indanthrene yellow mixed with cadmium yellow [12]. Field's madder yellow, a preparation from madder root, was described in 1835 as bright and resembling Indian yellow, though Salter later said he never made a comparable one [4].

sections.title: In European painting and color theory
sections.body:
For colormen and theorists the pigment was a pure yellow. Ball reports that George Field held that the purest hues were lemon yellow (earlier, Indian yellow), red madder and ultramarine [8]. Gage records that Field used ultramarine, madder and Indian yellow in his earliest color diagrams [10].

Later theorists kept using it for experiments. Ball lists it among the older pigments Ogden Rood tested, with gamboge, red lead, carmine lake and Prussian blue, and notes that Seurat and Signac may not have noticed how those pigments differed from their own [9]. Ball's survey of the painter's yellows names it first, ahead of gamboge, Naples yellow, orpiment and lead-tin yellow [13]. Of these, [[orpiment]] is the one that is also in our color list, a poisonous arsenic yellow [7].

Indian yellow is also easy to confuse with the names around it. A true gamboge is a resin, and orpiment is a mineral, while [[gallstone-yellow]] was made from ox gallstones, and St Clair notes that Indian yellow was probably made from urine [3]. A painter who wanted a warm gold in the 1800s could pick from all of them [3][13].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, holds the swatch color as a clear presence (within a color distance of six, over at least five per cent of the canvas) in 520 works, or 2.2 per cent [15]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a look-alike, not a pigment test [15].

India stands out. The color covers 63 of the 721 Indian works, four times the archive's rate [15]. In the Mughal school it is 21 of 168, in Rajput 12 of 97 and in Pahari 13 of 118, all five to six times the baseline [15]. The two clearest examples are the court portrait [[painting:cma-170846|Portrait of Raja Ram Singh of Amber]] and [[painting:cma-155590|Vishnu and Lakshmi on Garuda]], where the color covers more than half the picture [15]. The reading fits what the books say of Rajasthani and Pahari painters [3][7].

The Western numbers need care, because a match is only a look-alike hue [15]. The hue turns up most in the fourteenth century, in 18 of 251 works, or 7.2 per cent, at 3.3 times the archive baseline, long before the pigment reached Europe [15][1]. That is probably gold leaf and aged varnish, not Indian yellow, which the books place in Europe centuries later [1][3]. Among painters the highest rates are [[painter:jean-baptiste-greuze|Greuze]] (3 of 12 works), [[painter:pietro-perugino|Perugino]] (3 of 16) and [[painter:caravaggio|Caravaggio]] (6 of 47), but counts this small are suggestive, not conclusive [15]. In Impressionism, 140 works, none carry it [15].

Inside a painting it usually plays a highlight: 94 per cent of the matches are among the lightest areas of their picture [15]. Its closest company in other works is [[marigold]], [[apricot]], [[mustard]] and [[ochre]] [15].

In printed English the name rose in the 1850s, peaked around the 1880s and 1890s, the decades of Mukharji's letter, and by the 1960s had fallen to about a tenth of its peak [16]. Where to look: in a Rajput or Pahari miniature, find the warm gold that sits at the edge of orange, and notice how it glows beside a flat blue like Krishna's skin [2][15].

origin.named_after: India, where the pigment was made (the Indian names were piuri, peori and gogili)
origin.first_recorded: Indian use by about the 15th century (Ball); in Dutch paintings of the 17th century; name 1735 per Maerz and Paul
origin.source: Ball, Bright Earth, ch. 14; Pigment Compendium, p. 206

other_languages.name: gogili, from a Persian term read as "cow earth"

questions.q: What gives Indian yellow its color?
choices: A calcium or magnesium salt of euxanthic acid
questions.answer: A calcium or magnesium salt of euxanthic acid

questions.q: True or false: historians have found the law that banned Indian yellow for cruelty to cows.
Why does our archive find the Indian yellow swatch so often in 1300s European paintings, centuries before the pigment arrived?
choices: It is a look-alike, probably gold leaf and aged varnish
questions.answer: It is a look-alike, probably gold leaf and aged varnish

openers: The colorant of Indian yellow is a salt of euxanthic acid, and the famous mango-cow recipe rests on one report from 1883 [4][3].
Nobody has found the law that supposedly banned Indian yellow for cruelty, and Mirzapur has no memory of making it [2][3].
Look for it in Rajput and Pahari miniatures: it covers 12 of 97 Rajput works in our archive, about six times the baseline [15].

issues: Origin date: Ball says 15th c. India, Finlay late 16th c. Persian invention
First Western use: Ball 17th c. Dutch, St Clair late 1700s
Ban: Ball and Jarman assert; Finlay, St Clair, Compendium cannot find records
Mukharji account single-source; Finlay found no local memory
Archive 1300s peak is a look-alike (gold/varnish), not the pigment
Reworded phrase shared with Ball (Dutch 17th c.)
Lede softened: 'most famous story' was an overstatement
